paras: The attempted lynching of John McCray took place in Peoria, Illinois, on June 23-24, 1903, when crowds of a thousand or more besieged the jails to seize McCray, a Black man accused of killing Detective William E. Murphy. Police and deputies held the crowds off, and the sheriff secretly moved McCray to Galesburg. McCray was later convicted and hanged legally on December 11, 1903, still denying the killing, after a reprieve that a Peoria judge said fed "the spirit of mob law."

According to the wire, McCray shot Murphy at Water and Eaton streets about 10 p.m. on June 23 as the detective served a burglary warrant; Murphy died within twenty minutes. The Peoria Herald-Transcript, quoted by the Canton Weekly Register, put the shooting at Water and Fayette streets about 9 o'clock and said the complaint against McCray was for stealing coal.

Within an hour of McCray's arrival at the city jail, a crowd of "at least 1,000 men and boys" demanded the prisoner from the chief of police, who refused. As the fire department made a decoy run past the jail and the city's lights were shut off, officers moved McCray to the county jail in the dark. The crowd soon surrounded the county jail amid rumors of a second mob forming in Murphy's neighborhood. Sheriff Potter posted deputies and police with Winchesters and revolvers in front, ordered to fire if anyone tried to enter. Lacking a leader, the crowd began to break up shortly before 1 a.m. and had gone by 3 a.m.

Shortly after noon on June 24, Sheriff Potter and two deputies took McCray out a rear door and by carriage and train to the Galesburg jail. That morning several Black men jailed for petty offenses were moved to the workhouse "in order that no mistake might be made" if a mob broke in. That evening a larger crowd gathered, and State's Attorney Teft and Circuit Judge Green addressed it, promising a special grand jury and a speedy trial. A committee of six was allowed to search the jail, and when it reported McCray gone the crowd dispersed. The next morning McCray was hanged in effigy in the courthouse square, and a battering ram of telegraph poles was found behind the jail.

A special grand jury was called, and in early October McCray was found guilty of murder and sentenced to hang on October 30. Governor Yates granted a thirty-day reprieve on affidavits claiming new evidence, and McCray told the sheriff, "Again I swear before my Maker that I did not kill Murphy." A Peoria dispatch said that on October 30, the original execution date, seventy-five of Murphy's friends asked his brother to lead an assault on the jail and dispersed when he refused. Judge Theodore N. Green, who presided at the trial, said from the bench that the governor was doing more than anything else "to increase the spirit of mob law." McCray was hanged in the Peoria county jail at 9:05 a.m. on December 11, protesting his innocence; a later report noted that "No one saw the shooting."

White papers nationwide ran the Peoria wire under headlines such as "Mob Threatens to Lynch Negro Desperado," praising the officers. Follow-ups ran as "Lynching Only in Effigy" and "Lynching Averted," and the Canton Weekly Register cited the Peoria crowd in an editorial blaming lynching on "savage thirst for blood."

In November the Montgomery Advertiser reprinted a Milwaukee Free Press editorial, "Feeding the Mob Spirit," arguing that sparing a man who admitted the crime invited the next lynching. It said a "large delegation" of Black men had gone with his attorney to the governor and that the real consideration was "the negro vote."

Black papers carried the siege only as brief wire items: the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate's "Police Keep Back Mob," a Baltimore Afro-American special repeating "negro desperado," and the St. Louis Palladium's account of the Galesburg removal; none commented on the trial or hanging.

Crowd estimates ran from 1,000 in the first wire to "several thousand" in the Rock Island Argus and 3,000 in a weekly digest. The Milwaukee Free Press said McCray admitted the killing, but Peoria reports quoted his repeated denials.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John McCray
bases: Crowds of a thousand or more demanded McCray at the city jail and besieged the county jail to lynch him after the shooting of a detective, but officers held them off and moved him away (A1, A3, A12); a second planned jail assault in October was abandoned (A18).

A crowd far larger than three tried to seize McCray to avenge the killing of Detective Murphy, but he was not taken (A1, A3, A12); he was later hanged under a court sentence, which is a legal execution, not a lynching (A15, A24).

Independent wire, local Illinois and Black-press reports agree that a large crowd demanded McCray and surrounded the jails on June 23-24 and was held off by police and deputies (A1, A6, A7, A12); the October 30 plan rests on one dispatch (A18).

accounts.gist: McCray shot Murphy 'without a moment's warning' when told he was under arrest on a burglary warrant; a mob of 1,000 demanded him and was outwitted by a fire-department ruse and darkened streets.

accounts.label: Peoria Herald-Transcript (via Canton Weekly Register)
accounts.gist: The arrest was for stealing coal; the crowd swarmed through city hall 'swearing vengeance' but lacked a leader and left by 3 a.m.

accounts.label: Black press wire items
accounts.gist: Police foiled a mob that stormed the jail; officers spirited McCray to Galesburg and moved Black petty prisoners out of the jail.

accounts.label: Judge Green
accounts.gist: A mob stormed city hall and the county jail 'for two nights'; the governor's reprieve fed mob law.

accounts.label: Milwaukee Free Press editorial (reprinted)
accounts.gist: McRae admitted the crime; a mob was held off on the promise of a speedy trial; the reprieve, won by a Black delegation, invites future lynchings.

accounts.label: McCray
accounts.gist: He swore he did not kill Murphy and that 'his life had been lied away', to the end.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Mob Threatens to Lynch Negro Desperado' and 'Lynching Averted' cast McCray as a 'negro desperado' and the officers as heroes of a 'clever ruse'.
The Canton Weekly Register's 'No Justification for Lynchers' used the Peoria crowd to argue that lynching was 'savage thirst for blood', not distrust of courts.
The Montgomery Advertiser and Milwaukee Free Press opposed the mob but called the reprieve 'Feeding the Mob Spirit' and laid it to 'the negro vote'.
Judge Green, quoted by the Rock Island Argus, said the governor was increasing 'the spirit of mob law' by staying a lawful sentence.

The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate, Baltimore Afro-American and St. Louis Palladium printed short wire items ('Police Keep Back Mob', 'Negro Kills Detective', 'Negro Spirited From Peoria') without comment.

record_check.dossier: The jail sieges took place the night of June 23-24, 1903, with a second crowd on the evening of June 24; October 30 was the original execution date and the day of an abandoned plan by 75 of Murphy's friends.
One person, John McCray, also printed as Billy McRay, McRae and McCrea.
Accused of shooting Detective William E. Murphy while Murphy was arresting him on a burglary warrant or a coal-theft complaint.
Unnamed crowd of Peoria 'men and boys' (1,000 to several thousand), with recruits rumored from Murphy's neighborhood; in October, 'friends of Murphy'.
Siege and threat are supported; add hanging in effigy and the search of the jail by a crowd committee.

record_check.record: Mob stormed the jail ... McRae later tried, convicted and sentenced to hang.
record_check.dossier: Correct as far as it goes, but the storming was in June, not October, and McCray was hanged legally at Peoria on December 11, 1903, after a reprieve.
Wide white wire coverage June 24-27 plus three Black papers (Wisconsin Weekly Advocate, Baltimore Afro-American, St. Louis Palladium); follow-ups in October-December.
